source_text: Πολλῶν δὲ ὄντων τῶν εἰς τὴν προκειμένην ἐξέτασιν χρησιμωτέρων, παραιτοῦμαι δὴ νῦν τοὺς καταφεύγοντας ἐπὶ τὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἔργα καὶ τοὺς τούτων δημιουργοὺς ἀνθρώπους, οἳ τὰ συντριβέντα τῶν ἔργων ἢ χρόνῳ παλαιωθέντα ἢ καὶ ἄλλως διαφθαρέντα καινουργεῖν ἀδυνατοῦσιν, εἶτα ἐξ ὁμοίου τοῖς κεραμεῦσι καὶ τέκτοσι δεικνύναι πειρωμένους τὸ καὶ τὸν θεὸν μήτ᾿ ἂν βουληθῆναι μήτε βουληθέντα δυνηθῆναι νεκρωθὲν ἢ καὶ διαλυθὲν ἀναστῆσαι σῶμα, καὶ μὴ λογιζομένους ὅτι διὰ τούτων τοῖς χειρίστοις ἐξυβρίζουσιν εἰς θεόν, συνεξισοῦντες τῶν πάντη διεστηκότων τὰς δυνάμεις, μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ τῶν ταύταις χρωμένων τὰς οὐσίας καὶ τὰ τεχνητὰ τοῖς φυσικοῖς. Περὶ μὲν οὖν τούτων σπουδάζειν οὐκ ἀνεπιτίμητον· ἠλίθιον γὰρ ὡς ἀληθῶς τὸ τοῖς ἐπιπολαίοις καὶ ματαίοις ἀντιλέγειν. Μακρῷ γε μὴν ἐνδοξότερον καὶ πάντων ἀληθέστατον τὸ φῆσαι τὸ παρὰ ἀνθρώποις ἀδυνατὸν παρὰ θεῷ δυνατόν. Εἰ δὲ δἰ αὐτῶν τούτων ὡς ἐνδόξων καὶ διὰ πάντων τῶν μικρῷ πρόσθεν ἐξητασμένων δείκνυσιν ὁ λόγος δυνατόν, εὔδηλον ὡς οὐκ ἀδύνατον. Ἀλλὰ μὴν οὐδ᾿ ἀβούλητον.
thought_title: God's power is not limited like human craftsmen's
orientation: Athenagoras is opening his argument by answering critics who compare God's ability to raise the dead with human artisans' inability to repair broken works.
pass_a_gloss: Though many things are more useful for the proposed examination, I now reject those who flee to the works of humans and to the human makers of these, who are unable to make new the broken works or those aged by time or also otherwise destroyed, then from the similar case with potters and carpenters try to show that God neither would wish nor, having wished, would be able to raise a dead or also dissolved body, and do not reckon that through these things they insult God with the worst insults, making equal the powers of things wholly separated, and rather also the substances of those using these powers and the artificial things with the natural things. To be zealous about these things, then, is not free from blame; for it is truly foolish to speak against superficial and vain things. But by far more reputable and truest of all is to say that what is impossible among humans is possible with God. And if through these very things, as reputable, and through all the things examined a little before, the argument shows it possible, it is quite clear that it is not impossible. But neither is it unwilled.

choices.why: The verb here means to decline or dismiss an argument or approach, not merely to ask or beg; 'reject' captures the dismissive force toward the critics' method.

choices.term: καταφεύγοντας ἐπὶ τὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἔργα
choices.english: those who flee for refuge to the works of humans
choices.why: The participle carries the idea of taking refuge in a weak analogy; 'flee for refuge' preserves the rhetorical charge that critics retreat to human examples.
The compound verb emphasizes the act of equating things that belong together in the comparison; 'making equal together' keeps the force of the prefix.

choices.english: the artificial things with the natural things
choices.why: The contrast is between products of craft and products of nature; 'artificial' and 'natural' render the philosophical distinction clearly.
The adjective is a litotes; rendering it as 'not free from blame' preserves the negative form and the sense that such zeal is blameworthy.
The glossary does not cover this term, but 'unwilled' keeps the privative alpha and the sense of not being willed by God, matching the argument's contrast between possible and willed.

pass_b_english: Many considerations would be more useful for the present inquiry, but for now I reject those who flee for refuge to the works of humans and to the human makers of those works. These makers cannot renew their works when they are broken, aged by time, or destroyed in some other way, and then from this likeness to potters and carpenters they try to show that God either would not wish or, if he did wish, would not be able to raise up a body that has died or been dissolved. They do not reckon that by these arguments they insult God in the worst way, making equal together the powers of things that are entirely distinct—or rather, making equal the substances of those who use these powers, and the artificial things with the natural things. To be zealous about such people, then, is not free from blame, for it is truly foolish to argue against superficial and empty objections. Yet it is far more honorable and truest of all to say that what is impossible for humans is possible for God. And if the argument shows through these very things, as reputable, and through all that was examined a little earlier, that it is possible, then it is clear that it is not impossible. Nor, indeed, is it unwilled.

last_rejected.quote: These makers cannot renew their works when they are broken, aged by time, or destroyed in some other way, and then from this likeness to potters and carpenters they try to show
last_rejected.source_quote: οἳ τὰ συντριβέντα τῶν ἔργων ἢ χρόνῳ παλαιωθέντα ἢ καὶ ἄλλως διαφθαρέντα καινουργεῖν ἀδυνατοῦσιν, εἶτα ἐξ ὁμοίου τοῖς κεραμεῦσι καὶ τέκτοσι δεικνύναι πειρωμένους
last_rejected.why: English makes 'from this likeness' modify the critics' argument, but Greek says they try to show from the likeness (i.e., by analogy) that God cannot raise the dead.
last_rejected.fix: who cannot renew works broken, aged by time, or otherwise destroyed, and then try from this likeness to potters and carpenters to show
last_rejected.ruling: ἐξ ὁμοίου means 'from the likeness/analogy'; English 'from this likeness' conveys the same analogical reasoning adequately.

last_rejected.quote: making equal together the powers of things that are entirely distinct—or rather, making equal the substances of those who use these powers, and the artificial things with the natural things
last_rejected.source_quote: συνεξισοῦντες τῶν πάντη διεστηκότων τὰς δυνάμεις, μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ τῶν ταύταις χρωμένων τὰς οὐσίας καὶ τὰ τεχνητὰ τοῖς φυσικοῖς
last_rejected.why: English 'things that are entirely distinct' obscures that τῶν πάντη διεστηκότων refers to the powers (and their users), not generic 'things'; 'artificial things with natural things' inverts Greek's 'artificial to natural'.
last_rejected.fix: equating the powers of those utterly different—or rather the substances of those who use them, and artificial with natural
last_rejected.ruling: τῶν πάντη διεστηκότων modifies τὰς δυνάμεις; 'things' is a reasonable rendering. 'With' vs 'to' for τοῖς is minor.

last_rejected.quote: To be zealous about such people, then, is not free from blame
last_rejected.source_quote: Περὶ μὲν οὖν τούτων σπουδάζειν οὐκ ἀνεπιτίμητον
last_rejected.why: English 'zealous about such people' misreads σπουδάζειν as caring about people, but here it means to labor/argue over these matters; 'not free from blame' weakens the sense of blameworthiness.
last_rejected.fix: To labor over these matters, then, is not without blame
last_rejected.ruling: σπουδάζειν περὶ τούτων can mean 'be zealous about these matters'; 'not free from blame' fairly renders οὐκ ἀνεπιτίμητον.

last_rejected.why: English 'unwilled' is awkward and potentially misleading; ἀβούλητον means 'not willed' or 'not desired', i.e., God does not lack the will for it.
last_rejected.fix: Nor, indeed, is it not willed
last_rejected.ruling: ἀβούλητον = 'unwilled'; the rendering is accurate. Awkwardness is stylistic, not a meaning change.
